description: The Resolver interface (#619): resolution — importing a project's schema/activity modules to produce contract DTOs — is the one genuinely language-bound control-plane layer. This document names it as a transport-shaped interface: in-process implementations bind these operations directly; a subprocess or network resolver exchanges exactly these JSON messages. Responses are named references into the control-plane contract — resolution returns exactly what the API serves, never new shapes.

transport.request: {"operation": <name>, "params": {…}} — params per operation below; an optional "id" echoes back on the response for request/response pairing over a stream
transport.error_shape: ApiError from the control-plane contract (controlplane/openapi.v1.json#/components/schemas/ApiError) PLUS the HTTP status the API would answer with: config/validation failures carry the raising exception's class name at 422, unknown ids are NotFound at 404 — a resolver failure is the same wire object (and status) the API would serve, so a control plane forwards both instead of translating.
transport.subprocess_framing: A subprocess resolver (#642) speaks newline-delimited JSON over stdio: one boot readiness line {"event": "ready", "resolver_version": "1", "runtime": <runtime>}, then one request object per stdin line and exactly one response object per stdout line, in order. The process is long-lived; every request is resolved with per-request freshness (nothing is cached across requests). Diagnostics go to stderr, never stdout.

params.manifest_path: string, required — the project manifest the resolver runtime can import

resolve_plan.response_schema: inline (below) — the plan is a binding-profile artifact, not a control-plane read DTO

response.plan: object, required — the resolved WorkflowPlan exactly as the runtime's generic workflow interprets it; the control plane treats it as opaque and dispatches it verbatim
response.task_queue: string, required — the resolved (environment-overlaid) task queue the execution starts on
response.spec_digest: string, required — the plan digest stamped into the execution memo (typeflux_spec_digest)
response.workflow_name: string, required — the workflow's logical name (memo typeflux_workflow)
response.version_label: string | null — workflow.version when declared (memo typeflux_workflow_version)
response.search_attribute: string | null — the keyword search attribute carrying the logical name on start, when configured

resolve_plan.profile_note: BINDING-PROFILE-SCOPED: this operation exists for binding profiles that dispatch the plan as a start argument (temporal-binding ts-plan-argument, start_args [plan, input]). A resolver for a runtime whose profile registers the plan into a versioned workflow type instead (python-versioned-type — its digest algorithm typeflux-yaml-graph-v1 is not even the plan's typeflux-yaml-plan-v1; the ABIs are deliberately divergent, #618) answers {ok: false, status: 422} with an ApiError explaining that its profile dispatches no plan. That rejection IS the operation's implementation for such runtimes — wired, not dead spec.

coverage_note: The four read operations plus resolve_plan are the complete language-bound resolution surface (resolve_plan added with the subprocess slice, #642: plan-as-argument dispatch needs the raw plan on the wire, which no read DTO carries). Six further routes import project modules today only to derive resolved identity or effective config — executions/versions/workers (registered workflow type, spec digest, task queue) and connections/correlation (resolved runtime/observability config, trace hints) — all of which resolve_bundle already returns (BundleWorkflowIdentity, runtime_effective, links); behind this interface they decompose into resolve_bundle output + binding-driver visibility operations (temporal-binding contract) or neutral probes, with no resolver operation of their own. Environment/policy/profile reads are pure YAML (never import project modules) and are deliberately outside this interface; deployment verification reuses resolve_bundle.
runtime_note: A resolver resolves projects of exactly one language runtime (its own). The registry declares each project's runtime (#619 slice 2); a control plane asked to resolve a project whose runtime it has no resolver for fails closed with a structured unsupported-runtime error, never garbage. Per-runtime multiplexing (#642): a control plane may hold one resolver per runtime and dispatches by the registry entry's declared runtime; its supported-runtime set is the union of its resolvers'. A CONFIGURED resolver that is dead or unresponsive is a 500-class server fault (the operator wired a resolver that is not serving), never a silent unsupported-runtime 501.
